The present appeal was preferred by the appellant on 27.09.2017 and was assigned to the then learned ASJ/FSSA Court and after administrative directions vide order no. 12072-12106/ Judl.
/NDD/PHC/ND dated 01.10.2019 it was assigned to this court for disposal of the same as per law.

By way of present appeal, the appellant Sarvan herein has challenged the judgment dated 28.08.2017 and order on the point of sentence dated 31.08.2016 passed by the then learned ACMM-II, PHC, New Delhi vide which the appellant/accused was held guilty for commission of offences punishable under sections 16(1A) r/w Section 7 of PFA Act, 1954, the appellant was awarded a sentence to undergo Simple Imprisonment for 01 year as well as to pay fine of Rs.30,000/- for commission of aforesaid offences and in dafault of payment of fine to undergo Simple Imprisonment of 15 days.
Benefit of Section 428 Cr.P.C, if any, applicable was given to him.
The appellant was summoned by the learned trial court vide order dated 31.07.2008 for 10.03.2009 to face trial.

After filing his appearance, the appellant did not opt to file an application under section 13(2) of the PFA Act thereby exercising his right to get the second counterpart of the sample analyzed from the Sarvan vs Delhi Administration/ on 14 October, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/92493974/

Thereafter matter was listed for pre-charge evidence, wherein the complainant examined PW-1 Sh. S.S. Parihar,the then SDM/LHA, PW2 Sh. B.P.Saroha and PW-3 Sh. D.N.Verma, Field Assistant.

6. On the basis of testimony of PW-1 Sh.S.S. Parihar and PW2 Sh.B.P. Saroha, on 07.06.2010 charge was framed against the accused for commission of offences punishable u/s 7/16(1A) of PFA Act for violation of provisions of Sub clause (a)(j) and(m)of Section 2(ia) of PFA Act alleging therein that on 15.03.2008 at about 01.00 p.m, appellant being the Vendor cum Proprietor of M/s Sarvan Store,
Bharthal Road near Bijwasan Railway Station, Bijwasan sold for analysis

thesample consisted of approximately 1500 grams of "Moong Ki Chilka" ready for sale, taken from an open gunny bag bearing no label declaration to FI Sh. Dharam Pal Singh on payment of Rs. 48/- in the presence of LHA and witness and the sample commodity was analyzed by Public Analyst vide her report No.PFA/Enf./703/2008 dated 02.04.2008 and opined that the sample is adulterated because it is coloured with synthetic colouring matter viz Tartrazine and Brillant Blue FCF and thereby he violated the provisions of sub-clause (a)(j) and (m) of Section 2(ia) of PFA CA no. 263/16 Sarvan Vs.
Delhi Admn /Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 4 of 13 Act, 1954 punishable under section 16(1A) of PFA Act, 1954 read with Section 7 of the PFA Act to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
6.1 During trial after the examination and detailed cross examination of three witnesses i.e. PW1 Sh.
S.S. Parihar, the then SDM/LHA, PW2 Sh. B.P.Saroha ( Food Inspector) and PW-3 Sh. D.N.Verma (
Food Inspector), prosecution evidence was closed and matter was fixed for Statement of accused .
7. The statement of accused was recorded under section 313 Cr.PC in which accused pleaded his innocence and admitted the sample proceedings, yet claimed that he had purchased 5kg dal/ the food article from market from one M/S Yadav Stores ; had no bill for the same ; admitted receipt of intimation letter and did not prefer to lead defence evidence.
7.1

After hearing the arguments of both the parties, appellant was convicted by the learned trial court for commission of offence punishable under section punishable u/s 7/16(1)(a) PFA Act for violation of Section 2(ia)(a) (j) and (m) of PFA Act, 1954 8.

The learned trial court in its impugned judgment dated 28.08.2017 observed that the samples had been collected according to the prescribed procedures from the vendor cum Proprietor/ appellant premises, on analyzing the sample, it was opined vide PA report that the food sample is adulterated,
appellant had sold adulterated food in violation of Section 2(ia)(a) (j) and ( m) of PFA Act and has committed the offence punishable u/s 7/16(1A) PFA Act.
The appellant was accordingly convicted and sentenced by the learned CA no. 263/16 Sarvan Vs. Delhi Admn /Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 5 of 13 trial court
and aggrieved by the said judgment and order on quantum of sentence dated 31.08.2017, the present appeal has been preferred by the appellant.
9.(I) The appellant has assailed the judgment and order on sentence passed by the learned trial court by urging various grounds.

3 II)

Alternatively, on the quantum of sentence, relying upon the new legislation, it was pleaded that the case of the appellant be considered sympathetically in the light of the preposition of law laid down by the Hon'ble Courts pursuant to coming of new legislation that is Food Safety & Standards Act.

10. During the course of argument on 06.10.2020, learned counsel for the appellant submitted that he is not challenging the merits of the case/ conviction decided by the learned trial court vide judgment dated 31.08.2017 and confining his appeal limited to the quantum of sentence only awarded to him vide order dated 31.08.2017 and to confirm his submissions, appellant has tender his statement in this regard and stated that prayed that a lenient view be taken against him by giving him the benefit of New Legislation as FSSAI.
11.

Learned counsel for the Delhi Admn./Food Department, objected to the same and submitted that according to statement of appellant, prosecution has established its case and he be sentenced with strict punishment in terms of old Act wherein minimum punishment is prescribed and no leniency be shown to the convict as it is a serious offence of food adulteration article / commodity CA no.
263/16 Sarvan Vs. Delhi Admn /Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 6 of 13 leading to hazardous consequences on the health or body of a person.

12. I have carefully gone through the available record as well as trial court record, have heard the submissions of learned counsel for both the parties at length and have also gone through the judgments relied upon by the parties.

13. In light of above submissions and discussion particularly when the statement of appellant is recorded, I find no valid and legal reasons to interfere with the well reasoned judgment of the learned trial court.

The findings of the learned trial court with respect to the conviction of the appellant for the offence punishable under 16(1A) of the PFA Act read with Section 7 of the PFA Act,
1954 are upheld.
II. Now Coming to the alternate plea of giving benefit of new legislation to the appellant/ accused.
14. It is argued by learned counsel for the appellant that on the date of pronouncement of judgment/order on sentence, the PFA Act, 1954 was repealed and new act had come into operation.

It is stated that the court should give benefit of the new legislation to the accused vide which the punishment provided under the old act has been diluted to a considerable extent, and that the offence for which the accused/appellant has been convicted now falls under the category of Unsafe Food punishable under section 59(1) of the new Act i.e Food and Safety Standards Act, 2006 (hereinafter called FSSA) punishable upto six months and fine of upto Rs. One lac only.

15. It was argued by learned counsel for the appellant that CA no. 263/16 Sarvan Vs. Delhi Admn /Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 7 of 13 appellant is a man of young age of 32 years, respectable person of society, has deep roots in the society, has responsibility towards his family consisting of wife and four minor children and old aged mother, is a vegetable vendor to earn his livelihood, not keeping good health, not involved in any other case, has furnished the details of the owner from where the 5 kg Moong Dal Chhilka was purchased and furnished the copy of the purchase bill of said dal and Sarvan vs Delhi Administration/

prayed that a lenient view be taken against him in light of the provisions of law under the new Act.

15.1 Further that case pertains to the year 2008, the appellant/accused has faced the trial almost 12 years which by itself is a sufficient punishment and the hardships faced by him caused him great mental agony, stress and rigors of trial during the said period.

It is also stated that now a days special circumstances exists due to outbreak of pandemic of Covid-19 and there are chances of appellant being infected with virus in case imprisonment of sentence is awarded to him.

15.2 In support of his submissions, learned counsel for appellant had relied upon the judgment of Nemi Chand Vs. State of Rajasthan ( Crl. Appeals No. 214 and 215 of 2016, vide order dated 10.03.2016, as corrected vide order dated 17.03.2016, as reported in 2016 (1) FAC 203 ) of Hon'ble Supreme Court and earlier judgment T Barai Vs. Henry 1983 ( ) SCC 177. 15.3 Per contra, learned SPP, strongly opposed the submissions advanced by learned counsel by addressing that the sentencing cannot be done in new Act since the definition of many offences are CA no. 263/16 Sarvan Vs. Delhi Admn /Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 8 of 13 changed in the new Act including this particular offence of which accused is charged.

entities.text: Nemi Chand Vs. State of Rajasthan ( Crl. Appeals No. 214 and 215 of 2016
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Definition of major offences like "adulteration" and "misbranding" have been changed.
Now FSSA have definition "substandard food", "food containing extraneous matter" "unsafe food" and misbranded food".
Due to this reason, the ingredients have changed and thus there is no way in which the old offences could be related to new offences.
15.4 As far as the objection of learned SPP is concerned, in the present case, the offence was that the article/food was found adulterated and was unfit for human consumption.

This was violation of Rules under PFA Rules and thus termed as adulteration in view of Section 2(1a)(a) (j) & (m) of the PFA Act and thus consequently punishable under section 16(1A) of PFA Act read with Section 7 of PFA Act.
15.5
That now in the FSSA such adulteration is termed as "unsafe food" in terms of Section 3(zz)(viii) of FSSA Act and violation thereof is punishable u/s 59(1) of FSSA.
So if we go through both these provisions of law a particular offence with a particular fact is mentioned with some other name but with same ingredients in the New FSSA Act.

- Sub-clause (viii) of 3(zz) FSSA Act is applicable where the colouring material or the preservative other than that specified in respect there of is found in the food article and no where the colouring material exceeds the prescribed limit.

15.6 Further, the charge in this case was framed for the said offences and there is no charge in which it is stated that the said CA no. 263/16 Sarvan Vs. Delhi Admn /Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 9 of 13 colour was injuries to health.

entities.text: CA no. 263/16 Sarvan Vs. Delhi Admn /Food Inspector (PFA)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Had it been the case, the charge should have been for the offence punishable u/s 16(1-A)(ii) of PFA Act.

15.7 Therefore, it is held that it is the ingredients which constitute an offence determines that whether it is the same offence but with new name or an altogether different offence, Here the offence of adding colour in the food article which was punishable u/s 16(1)(a) PFA Act is similar to the offence u/s 52 of FSSA Act, which is now punishable with simple imprisonment of six months and fine upto one lakh.
15.8 As far as the application of Nemi Chand Judgment (supra) is concerned, the same is based on the old judgment i.e. T Barai ( Supra) of Hon'ble Supreme Court.

sentences.text:
Judgment is as follows :
- (Para 25) It is settled both on authority and principle that when a later statute again describes an offence created by an earlier statute and imposes a different punishment or varies the procedure, the earlier statute is repealed by implication in Michell Vs.
Brown ( 1958) 120 ER 909, 912 : 32 LTOS 146:7 WR 80 Lord Campbell put the matter thus :
- "It is well settled rule of construction that, if a later statute again describes an ofence created by a former statute and affixes a different punishment, varying the procedure, the earlier statute is repealed by the later statute see also Smith Vs.
Benabo ( 1937) 1 ALL ER 523 : ( 1997) 1 KB 518: 156 LT 194"
- In Regina Vs. Youle ( 1861) 158 ER 311,315-16 : LT 299 : 9 WR 637 Martin B. said in the oft-quoted passage :
CA no. 263/16 Sarvan Vs. Delhi Admn /Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 10 of 13 - If a statute deals with a particular class of offences, and a subsequent Act is passed which deals with precisely the same offence, and a different punishment is imposed by the later Act, I think that, in effect, the legislature has declared that the new Act shall be substituted for the earlier Act."

entities.text:
Michell Vs.
Brown ( 1958) 120 ER 909, 912 : 32 LTOS 146:7 WR 80
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: - The rule is however subject to the limitation contained in Article 20(1) against ex post facto law providing for a greater punishment and has also no application where the offence described in the later Act is not the same as in the earlier Act i.e. when the essential ingredients of the two offences are different.

- Moreover, this particular aspect is stated as a illustration in the same judgment in Para 23 which is as follows :
- To illustrate, if Parliament were to reenact Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860 and provide that the punishment for an offence of murder shall be sentence for imprisonment for life instead of the present sentence of death or imprisonment for life, then it can not be that the courts would still award a sentence of death even in pending cases.
- Academic Reference can also be made to the letter dated 03.10.2017 of Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, produced before the court during the proceedings.

entities.label: ORG

sentences.text:
Vide said letter the said authority, in the light of judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Nemi Chand's Case ( supra ) issued an advisory to the Commissioners of Food Safety/Officers incharge of Food Safety to dispose of the long pending court cases filed under old PFA Act mainly concerning substandard and misbranding by imposing fine CA no. 263/16 Sarvan Vs. Delhi Admn /Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 11 Sarvan vs Delhi Administration/ on 14 October, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/92493974/
6 of 13 only.
- In view of the above mentioned discussion, it can be safely said that while considering on the point of sentence, the quantum of sentence in new Act i.e. FSSA is to be considered.

16. Thus analysing the facts of the case, taking note of the special circumstances of the case and the fact that accused has faced the trial of almost 12 years ; and also the fact that extraordinary circumstances exists due to outbreak of Covid 19 ; and in light of the above cited judgment and the judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Delhi titled as GNCT Vs. Jagdish Tyagi dated 11.10.2017 in my view the convict/ appellant is entitled to the benefit of new legislation.

Accordingly to meet the ends of justice, the sentence of the convict Sarvan as imposed by the learned trial court vide order dated 28.08.2017 stands modified to the extent that the order sentencing the appellant to undergo simple imprisonment of one year stands waived of to simple imprisonment for one day i.e. till rising of the court ; the sentence of fine is enhanced from Rs. 30,000/- to Rs.40,000/-
In default of payment of fine the appellant/convict shall undergo simple imprisonment for two months.
Senence modified accordingly.

17 Appellant/Convict is directed to deposit the fine amount within 30 days from the date of pronouncement of this judgment before the learned trial court and, if any, amount of fine was deposited by the appellant before the learned trial court same shall be adjusted accordingly.
18. The present appeal is disposed of accordingly in terms CA no. 263/16 Sarvan Vs. Delhi Admn /Food Inspector (PFA) Pages 12 of 13 thereof.
